segments.title: First clarinet and the metal clarinet now in a museum
segments.summary: Lewis describes his first cheap Albert-system clarinet bought for four dollars, its leather case, and the metal clarinet he bought during the Depression.

segments.title: Clarinet cracking, metal versus wood tone, Harry Pedler clarinet
segments.summary: He explains how clarinets crack and are repaired, and says he finds little tonal difference between metal and wood, naming the Harry Pedler clarinet.

segments.title: Albert versus Boehm system among New Orleans clarinetists
segments.summary: He lists New Orleans clarinetists who played Albert system and recalls briefly trying a Boehm system that Al Landry tried to sell him.

segments.title: A-clarinets and playing in different keys with Buddy Petit
segments.summary: He explains that cornetists sometimes played in A, forcing him to transpose, as in Maple Leaf Rag with Buddy Petit.

segments.title: Mouthpiece lay, reeds, and his father's goat-horn reed
segments.summary: Talk of mouthpiece lay and matching soft reeds to wide lays; Lewis's father tried to make a reed from goat horn.

segments.title: The turtle-shell banjo
segments.summary: Lewis recalls a man who made a banjo from a turtle shell that looked beautiful but lacked tone.

segments.title: How long reeds last, trimming and burning them
segments.summary: He describes reed lifespan, his habit of cutting reeds with a coin and a match, and views on reed cutters.

segments.title: Wood, rubber and metal clarinets compared
segments.summary: He prefers wood, compares rubber, and relays Bill Russell's remark that material makes no tonal difference; his museum clarinet was out of line.

segments.title: Albert versus Boehm keys and technique
segments.summary: Discussion of simple Albert, Boehm system being easier, Raymond Burke's rubber bands on keys, and use of side keys.

segments.title: Tone, avoiding popping and playing softly
segments.summary: Lewis explains his light tone, dislike of popping reeds, and how blowing softly with stiff reeds shaped his tone.

segments.title: Growling and the Paul Moser band
segments.summary: Short talk on growling, then Lewis recalls playing in a band led by Paul Moser with Kimber and Ernest Poirier.

segments.title: Trying plastic reeds
segments.summary: He tried plastic reeds but could not get the right tone.

segments.title: Choice of reed and learning stiff reeds playing funerals
segments.summary: He buys La Vore reeds and learned to like stiff reeds playing funeral parades before taking up E-flat clarinet; Joe Watson is mentioned.

segments.title: Parade days, Joe Watson and Al Landry's E-flat clarinet
segments.summary: He describes all-day May parades, fairground bands, and how Al Landry of the Eureka band brought him an E-flat clarinet.

segments.title: Changing embouchure after bleeding lips at jitney dances
segments.summary: Lewis explains he started with lips over his teeth, then switched to biting the top lip after his lips bled playing jitney dances.

segments.title: Effect of the embouchure on tone, calluses and wear
segments.summary: He says the change did not alter his tone, discusses the double embouchure, calluses, and teeth wearing a crescent in the mouthpiece.

segments.title: Losing teeth, dentures and playing again
segments.summary: Lewis tells of having teeth pulled in New York, getting dentures put in immediately, and returning to play within days.

segments.title: Playing for audiences and how recording sessions should run
segments.summary: He prefers playing before people, recalls Norman Granz letting the band pick tunes, and argues the first take is best.

segments.title: Not reading music; Professor Delmo and a Boston teacher
segments.summary: Lewis says he never learned to read music, took two lessons from Professor Delmo, and recalls a Boston teacher's warning.

segments.title: Breathing from the diaphragm and drummers' tempo
segments.summary: He advises breathing from the diaphragm, then comments on drummers and keeping tempo.

segments.title: Reaching high notes and testing them before playing
segments.summary: He says his fingers know what comes next and describes testing a high note and adjusting the reed beforehand.

segments.title: Practice habits and the low versus high register
segments.summary: He practises in the low register, argues for its beauty, and discusses weaving high and low with Acker Bilk and Bill Shea.

segments.title: Playing at funerals: hymns, soft playing and Washington Street Cemetery
segments.summary: Lewis describes funeral marches and hymns, playing softly, and a woman at Washington Street Cemetery who had a man stopped.

segments.title: Whether he plays sharp, and tuning to pianos
segments.summary: They discuss critics saying he plays sharp, and he explains tuning problems with flat pianos and horns.

segments.title: First tunes learned and Creole-speaking mother
segments.summary: Lewis recalls early tunes such as the rag-and-bones song his mother hummed, and says his mother spoke Creole.
